claims.text: Hibbard’s 1962 paper on combinatorial properties of certain trees is titled with applications to searching and sorting, and is the reference for the standard deletion procedure in an ordered binary tree: a node with two children is removed by replacing it with the node holding the smallest key in its right subtree.

source.title: Hibbard, T. N., Some combinatorial properties of certain trees with applications to searching and sorting, Journal of the ACM 9(1):13-28, January 1962

claims.text: That replacement preserves the ordering because there are no keys between the removed node’s key and its successor’s key.

source.title: Hibbard, T. N., Some combinatorial properties of certain trees with applications to searching and sorting, Journal of the ACM 9(1):13-28, January 1962

beats.broke: hierarchical data has no single order in which to visit it, so any procedure that must touch everything has to choose one, and the choice is usually made by accident
beats.fix: three depth-first orders distinguished only by when the node is visited relative to its children, plus a breadth-first order by level
beats.cost: the orders are not interchangeable, and a traversal written for one purpose produces confidently wrong results when reused for another
beats.interview: how to choose a traversal order without memorising which is which
